titulo: Why does the other checkout line always seem faster?
destinatario: se lo manda alguien que siempre cambia de fila en el súper a su amigo que siempre elige la fila equivocada, para decirle que no es solo mala suerte
fuentes: Queueing theory: its first paper, from 1909, is by Danish engineer Agner Krarup Erlang, on telephone calls in Copenhagen (MacTutor, University of St Andrews)
Queueing model: one single line feeding all registers (M/M/c) gives an average wait less than or equal to one line per register (c x M/M/1), with the same people and the same registers
Perception: Qminder, popular source, so it is stated as 'probably'

frases.texto: It always feels like the other checkout line moves faster. And it's not just bad luck.
When every register has its own line, one slow customer holds up everyone behind them.
With a single line feeding all the registers, that same customer delays just one register. The others keep going.

Queueing theory, which starts in nineteen oh nine with Danish engineer Agner Erlang, shows it: with the same registers and the same people, one single line gives an average wait that's shorter or equal.
And your brain probably plays a part too: you notice when the other line speeds up, and forget when it stalls.
Heads up: that's about the average. On a bad streak, you can still get the slow one.
Send this to the friend who switches lines three times.
